<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page detailed his grand, unfinished project to harmonize the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle; this page transitions into his minor works, his mastery of various rhetorical styles, and his formidable speed in absorbing both classical and Scholastic theology.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...only <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a list of his minor works.</note> an interpretation of the Lord's Prayer, and about fifty "Rules for Living Well." These rules were certainly too brief and not fully explained, for he had intended to expand them into many chapters if he had lived. He also composed two prayers to God: <margin>Music cultivated</margin> one in Tuscan rhythms <note>original: "rhithmis hetruſcis." Pico wrote poetry in the Italian vernacular (Tuscan), which was common among humanists of his era.</note> and the other in elegiac meter. He did this so that when he was worn out by heavier studies, he could soothe his mind by singing to the lyre. Indeed, in the first years of his youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised and the harmonies he noted with their proper arrangements were held in high regard. We also saw many other things in his chests, although they were unorganized, from which I believe something useful could be compiled, especially an exposition of the Psalms.

<margin>Multifaceted letters</margin> Furthermore, about fifty letters emerged, published at various times—some familiar, some doctrinal, and some encouraging—along with the oration which he was to have delivered in Rome if the disputation had been allowed to take place. This oration reflects a most sharp genius and most abundant learning, remarkable for a youth who was not yet twenty-four years old. This is true of all his writings, which provide us with the richest testimony of his most fertile eloquence. 

<margin>An approved character of speaking</margin> He always used a style that was highly commendable—not artificial, but natural, multifaceted, and varying according to the subject. Although he used up (as they say) the whole "perfume-box" of Isocrates <note>original: "Iſocratis myrotheciōn." This is a classical metaphor, used by Cicero, referring to a storehouse of refined rhetorical ornaments.</note>, he nevertheless preserved a cleanliness of style and the ornaments of majestic decorum. 

<margin>Kinds of speaking</margin> Indeed, those celebrated "kinds of speaking"—of which Gellius lists three and Macrobius four—can be gathered from his works without great effort. <margin>Copious, Brief, Dry, Flowery, and Rich</margin> There one finds the **copious** style in which Cicero usually rules; the **brief** which is ascribed to Sallust; the **dry** given to Fronto; and the **rich and flowery** in which they say Pliny and Symmachus indulged. But perhaps Brutus would not have called this copiousness "weak," nor Sallust "immoderate." An orator with right judgment will easily perceive Fronto’s "dryness" moistened, Sallust’s "brevity" extended, and the flowery richness of Pliny carried into a wider field. Add to these the "milky fountain" of Livy—perhaps without that "Paduanism" <note>original: "patauinitate." A famous ancient criticism of Livy by Asinius Pollio, suggesting his Latin had a regional Paduan accent or style.</note>—with many little flowers of Apuleius added.

Truly, he did not exercise himself here in philosophy merely borrowed from the Greeks, nor in "Attic Nights" <note>Refers to the *Noctes Atticae* by Aulus Gellius, a collection of miscellaneous notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note>, nor in fictional "Saturnalia" <note>Refers to the *Saturnalia* by Macrobius, a work of Virgilian criticism and antiquarian lore.</note> fabricated almost entirely to praise Virgil’s *Aeneid*, nor in Roman history, nor in a mere natural history empty of the deepest and most difficult speculations. Rather, he labored over that admirable "fabric of the world" <note>likely referring to his work on the creation, the *Heptaplus*.</note> and wore himself out in attacking the enemies of the holy Catholic Church and in eliminating the influence of astrologers. He labored in examining theological questions and in the harmony of Aristotle and Plato; he applied himself to explaining the sacred words of Scripture and devoted his energy to advising and encouraging his friends. 

Truly, he was so far from affecting this eloquence of which we speak that he rather condemned those who, searching too scrupulously for "painted allurements," devoted all the powers of their genius to investigating the origins of words. All these things turned many people even more toward admiration of him, because he had been engaged long and most deeply among the writings of those who did not profess Latin letters filled with the "flowers of eloquence" <note>This refers to the Scholastic theologians, whom humanists often criticized for their "barbarous" or unpolished Latin style.</note>. Let the excessive lovers of antiquity bear this with an even mind; for although these things are stated concisely, they are perhaps more true for the fact that men more learned than I—Ermolao Barbaro, Battista the Carmelite, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men—have declared them. 

<margin>Speed of reading</margin> He read through and excerpted from vast libraries of both Latin and Greek works with incredible speed; he passed over no commentaries unread, provided the opportunity was given. He had attained such a degree of knowledge concerning the ancient Doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe, even for one who had spent his whole life doing nothing but unrolling their works. But concerning the "modern" theologians who used that style commonly called "Parisian" <note>original: "Parīſienſem." This refers to Scholasticism, the dialectical and logical method of theology associated with the University of Paris.</note>, such judgment resided in him that if anyone suddenly asked him to unravel some abstruse and poorly explained question of theirs, he would open it with such fertility of genius and unlock it with such skill that [it seemed]...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense within his "Apologia." Having previously discussed the "de-acceptance" of the sinner by God, he now addresses the specific logical responses to the nature of sin and its eternal punishment.</meta>

-># APOLOGY<-

<margin>Responses which the author had given</margin>
...leading to an enduring state of guilt. <margin>First</margin> It must be understood that the nature of the offense is tied to the persistence of the will. <margin>Second</margin> While the act itself is transitory, the turning away from the Divine remains. <margin>Third</margin> Therefore, the punishment is not for a past action that has ceased, but for a state of being that the soul refuses to abandon.

<margin>Question</margin>
If the act of sinning is finished in a moment, how can the punishment endure? 

<margin>Response</margin>
The response lies in the distinction between the act and the debt. Through sin <note>original: "peccato"</note>, the soul enters a state of debt that it cannot repay on its own. Unless the sinner repents, they remain in that sin <note>original: "peccato"</note> eternally. Thus, the infinity of the punishment corresponds to the infinity of the duration of the sin <note>original: "peccato"</note> itself within the soul of the damned. 

<margin>Note</margin>
It is important to note <note>original: "Nota"</note> that the gravity of the sin <note>original: "peccati"</note> is also considered infinite in a relative sense, because it is an offense against God, who is the Infinite Good.

<margin>Recapitulation</margin>
To summarize the argument: the sinner is not punished eternally for a finite moment of pleasure, but for an eternal persistence in that sin <note>original: "peccato"</note>. The duration of the penalty matches the duration of the guilt.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola provides a three-part defense and a formal question-and-answer session regarding the justice of eternal punishment. He argues that the "infinity" of Hell is a response to the sinner's eternal persistence in their state of sin rather than the brief duration of the sinful act itself.</summary>

<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Apologia, mortal sin, infinite punishment, divine justice, guilt, repentance, Scholasticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Apologia," where he defends his eleventh proposition: "There is no science that more certifies us of the divinity of Christ than Magic and Kabbalah." Having just finished his defense of the tenth proposition regarding the Eucharist, he is now rebutting the specific charge that this new claim is heretical or "scandalous."</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...is to be condemned, not mine, which is holy and Catholic. Third, let them tell me: what is this "bad meaning" <note>original: "malus sensus"; Pico is challenging the inquisitors to define exactly how his words could be interpreted as heretical.</note> which it could produce? Let them speak if they know; certainly, it is not possible to say, even if one wished to or tried to imagine, that a bad meaning arises from that proposition. For if there were one, it would perhaps be that someone might suspect me of wishing to say that the same miracles which Christ performed—at least regarding the physical deed itself—could be done through magic. But it is not permitted to suspect this of my conclusion because, immediately before it, I set down another conclusion: that the miracles of Christ could not be done by way of magic or Kabbalah. <note>original: "per uiā magiæ uel cabalæ." Pico is referring to his preceding thesis where he explicitly separates Christ’s divine power from any occult art. Kabbalah refers to the Jewish mystical tradition which Pico sought to synthesize with Christian theology.</note> Any other bad meaning that could be found or devised, I do not see; let them speak if they are able. Fourth, let them tell me: what kind of logical consequence is this? Does it hold in its matter or its form? <note>In scholastic logic, an argument was tested by its "matter" (content) and "form" (structure). Pico is mocking the lack of rigor in his accusers' reasoning.</note> "It is among the magical [conclusions], therefore it is to be condemned." <summary>Pico defends his thesis on magic and Kabbalah by arguing that his critics cannot find a truly heretical interpretation of his words, especially since he explicitly stated that Christ's miracles were not performed through magic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Oration on the Dignity of Man." Having just quoted Seneca to justify his eclecticism—refusing to be confined to a single "porch" or school of thought—Pico now details the specific, diverse traditions he has synthesized in his 900 theses, including Egyptian, Chaldean, and Hebrew sources, alongside his own original philosophical discoveries.</meta>

->ORATION<-

...one should be kept confined within a single porch. <note>Closing the note from the previous page: Pico refers to the *Stoa* or "porch" where the Stoics taught, using it as a metaphor for being trapped in a single philosophical school.</note>

And it was not enough for me, beyond the common schools of thought, to have added much regarding the Ancient Theology of the Egyptians <note>original: "Prisca Aegyptiorum theologia." This refers to the "Ancient Theology," a Renaissance belief that a single, true theology exists which threads through all religions and was given by God to man in antiquity.</note>, the dogmas of the Chaldeans, and the secret mysteries of the Hebrews, unless I also proposed many things discovered and thought out by myself regarding philosophical matters. 

And so that those who see them might appreciate not only the number, but also the novelty and variety of my propositions, I have proposed points concerning the harmony between Plato and Aristotle <margin>Plato & Aristotle</margin> <note>original: "de concordia Platonis et Aristotelis." The attempt to reconcile these two giants of Greek thought—who were often seen as opposites—was a hallmark of Pico's "syncretism," or the blending of different beliefs.</note>, which many previously believed in, but no one has sufficiently proven.

I have then proposed seventy-two new physical and metaphysical <term>Metaphysical</term> <note>Relating to the branch of philosophy that deals with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, substance, and cause.</note> propositions, entirely new. If anyone masters these, they will be able (unless I am mistaken) <note>original: "ni fallor." Pico uses this modest phrasing even while making an extremely bold claim about the power of his system.</note> to resolve any proposed question concerning natural or divine matters by a far different and much more certain path than the one taught in the common schools <margin>The Schools</margin> <note>The "schools" refer to the Scholastic universities of the time, which Pico often criticized for being too rigid or focused on logic-chopping rather than universal truth.</note>.

Nor should anyone wonder, Fathers <note>Pico is addressing the "Fathers" (the gathered clergy and scholars at Rome) who were meant to judge his public debate.</note>, that I—at such a young age, at which it has been permitted to few to even read the works of others—wish to bring forth a new philosophy <margin>A New Philosophy</margin>. 

Furthermore, I have proposed a new way of philosophizing through numbers, and I have brought back into the light the ancient and secret mysteries of the Hebrew Kabbalah <margin>The Kabbalah</margin> <note>The Kabbalah is a body of Jewish mystical and esoteric teachings. Pico was a pioneer in "Christian Kabbalah," believing these Jewish secrets could provide "proof" for the divinity of Christ.</note>, which I was the first among Latins <note>original: "primus ego ex Latinis." Pico claims to be the first Western/Latin scholar to bring these specific Hebrew traditions into the academic sphere of the Church.</note> to study.

<summary>Pico explains that his 900 theses are not just a collection of old ideas, but include his own "new philosophy" and a synthesis of Plato, Aristotle, and the Jewish Kabbalah. He claims his method offers a more certain path to truth than the traditional university education of his day.</summary>

<keywords>syncretism, Plato and Aristotle, Kabbalah, Scholasticism, Prisca Theologia, Renaissance philosophy, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</keywords>

Hanc autem aſſiduam meditationem & ſtabilitatem, ſeu permanentiam mentis in ſuperis (quemadmodum primo & tertio Volumine latiùs expoſui) peragere neſcit fragilis & terrena mortalium conditio, niſi in his carnis operibus (ſine quibus uita, & ſocietas humana ſtare & cuſtodiri nequit) quaſi in tenui quodā ſimulachro, & umbroſa archetypi imagine, ſupercœleſtia proſpiciat exemplaria, atq; iugi cogitatione æternæ Legis mandata contempletur: Alioquin ſeiungunt & diſtrahunt animum terrena hæc opera à ſupercœleſtium aquarum riuulis, & ab ipſa æternitatis origine. Iuxta illud Iacobi: Qui autem perſpexerit in Lege perfecta libertatis, & permanſerit in ea, non auditor obliuioſus, ſed factor operis, hic beatus in facto ſuo erit. Facilè igitur & externi operis beatitudo ex hoc maximè (ſi conſyderas) pendet, quòd operis factor (quaſi ſpeculi inſpector) exemplarem, & perfectæ libertatis proſpiciet Legem, & in ea manet, quam Apoſtolus ad Galatas per allegoriam ſeu Cabalā cœleſte testamentum, & liberam uocat matrem noſtram, quæ ſurſum est Ieruſalem. Si ergo factor operis illam perfectæ libertatis Legem, cuius umbram (ut ad Hebræos ſcribitur) habet Lex iſta mandatorum, minus perſpexerit, neq; in ea permanſerit, infœlix nimirum & miſer operato in facto ſuo erit: qui enim non ponit Deum (ut Pſaltes admonuit) in conſpectu ſuo, & à dextris ſuis: ſemper illius mox animus labitur, tenditq; in præceps & corruit. Propterea omne (inquit ueritatis Præco) quodcumq; facitis in uerbo aut in opere, omnia in nomine Domini noſtri Ieſu Chriſti, facite. Et Apoſtolus 2. Corinth. 10. In carne ambulantes, non ſecundum carnem militenur, & operemur. Hæc autē perficere & docere optimè nouerunt allegorizantes, qui ſingula externa opera, immò & uniuerſa ſacri eloqui uerba & elementa referunt tolluntq; ad ſuperos, ita ut per hanc operandi & contemplandi Legem, quaſi per cœleſtes ligones, & uomeres ipſum uigil agri colonus de ſiccaneo aridoq; hoc ſolo, effodiat, & eruat, & ad ſupercœleſtium aquarum riuulis atq; fluenta transplātet, unde locupletius fructum ſuo tempore prœstat, eiuſq; folia (ut canit Pſaltes) non computreſcant, & quicquid faciet proſperetur. Nos igitur ad rectam, & clariorem huius dogmatis intelligentiam, quartum hoc de Cœleſti Agricultura Volumen conſecimus, quo fidei & arcanæ ueritatis ſtudioſus ſœcundum agrum ſuum diligentiùs colere, uberioremq; fructum proferre, & facto ac opere explere queat, iuuante & dante incrementum Cœleſti Agricola Deo, cui ſit gloria & benedictio in ſæcula.

Duo itaq; præſens hoc Volumen complectitur. Primò introductorium proponit, quo neglecto nemo ad ueram & arcanam Cabaleorum ſeu allegorantium dogmatis agnitionem facilè peruenire poterit: quid enim nomen deſignet Cabale, quæ eius neceſſitas, & finis, qua etiam ratione hæc alia dogmata antecellat, quis modus docendi & ordo, quæ deniq; primariæ eius partes, planè oſtendit. Secundò de ſacris nominibus, eorumq; attributis paraphrasim & Epitome ſubnectit, quod de hallucinantium Iudæorum bibliotheca (ueluti ſplendidiſſimam facem de cæcutientis tediſerā manū) illuſtratis fidelium mentibus tradendum eripui & compendio perſtrinxi, quo facilè patebunt aditus ad ſacri eloqui penetralia, diuinorumq; nominum ſacramenta, unde quiuis perſpicax, & ſedulus Chriſtianæ pietatis cultor paruo quidem negocio allegorizantium dogmati initiari, in eoq; proficere, & erudiri poterit, diuina opitulante gratia, & indiuidua Trinitate alma: Cuius ſublimi & ineffabili, in quo omne genu flectitur, nomine inuocato, primam huius Voluminis partem aggredimur. Prius tamen mox ſequentem aduerſus obtrectatorem Cabalæ orationem, quæ præſenti negocio non parum intelligentiæ luminis affert, præponere hic libuit.

## PREFACE TO THE FOURTH VOLUME.

AFTER the uncultivated and neglected field of those practicing philosophy has been prepared and re-tilled; after the barren and rocky ground of the younger Jews has been cleared; and after the thorny field of certain wandering believers has been purged of thistles and weeds—it remains for me now to approach the fertile field of the faithful and devoted, to irrigate and enrich it. This field will be watered more abundantly when it has been adapted, with diligent care and study, to the spring of the super-celestial waters. Indeed, it will be more exquisitely prepared when the worker of the external labor performs everything in this dry and mortal soil—not according to the earthly sense and the letter, which kills—but rather through spiritual and mystical intelligence. For the letter (because it turns away and distracts from the heavenly life) kills; but the Spirit (as the Apostle says) gives life, and restores the soul to the origin of eternal life. Therefore, the greater the diligence and persistence with which one exercises the mind on higher things and fixes one's gaze there, the more copiously do the heavenly streams drip and irrigate, and God, the <term>Celestial Farmer</term> <note>original: "coelestis Agricola"; the central metaphor of Riccius’s work, portraying God as a gardener and spiritual study as cultivation</note>, generously gives the increase. 

However, the fragile and earthly condition of mortals does not know how to carry out this constant meditation and stability—or permanence of the mind—in higher things (as I have explained more extensively in the first and third Volumes), unless one looks upon the super-celestial patterns within these works of the flesh (without which human life and society cannot stand or be preserved). One must view them as if in a thin likeness and a shadowy image of the archetype, contemplating the commands of the eternal Law with unceasing thought. Otherwise, these earthly works separate and distract the soul from the rivulets of super-celestial waters and from the very origin of eternity. As James says: *But he who looks into the perfect Law of liberty and remains in it, being not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.* 

Therefore, the happiness of the external work easily depends mostly upon this (if you consider it): that the doer of the work (like one looking into a mirror) looks forward to the exemplary Law of perfect liberty and remains in it. The Apostle, in the letter to the Galatians, calls this Law—through allegory or <term>Cabala</term> <note>original: "Cabalā"; Riccius uses this term to mean a tradition of mystical or allegorical interpretation of Scripture</note>—the heavenly testament and our free mother, who is the Jerusalem above. If, therefore, the worker of the deed looks less upon that Law of perfect liberty (of which this Law of commandments has a shadow, as is written to the Hebrews), and does not remain in it, he will surely be unhappy and wretched in his labor. For he who does not set God (as the Psalmist warned) before his sight and at his right hand, his soul soon slips, tends toward the precipice, and falls. For this reason, the Herald of Truth <note>meaning St. Paul</note> says: *Whatever you do in word or in deed, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.* And the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 10 says: *Walking in the flesh, let us not war or work according to the flesh.* 

Those who use allegory know best how to perform and teach these things. They refer and raise every external work—and indeed all the words and elements of the sacred discourse—to the heavens. Thus, through this Law of working and contemplating, as if through celestial hoes and plowshares, the watchful tiller of the field digs into and clears this parched and dry soil, transplanting it to the rivulets and streams of super-celestial waters. From there, it brings forth fruit more abundantly in its own time, and its leaves (as the Psalmist sings) shall not wither, and whatever he does shall prosper. We, therefore, for the right and clearer understanding of this doctrine, have composed this fourth Volume on Celestial Agriculture, by which the student of faith and secret truth may be able to cultivate his fertile field more diligently, bring forth richer fruit, and fulfill it in deed and work, with the help and increase of God, the Celestial Farmer, to whom be glory and blessing forever.

This present Volume, then, embraces two things. First, it proposes an introduction, which, if neglected, no one will easily be able to reach a true and secret recognition of the teachings of the Cabalists or those who use allegory. It clearly shows what the name "Cabala" designates, what its necessity and goal are, by what reasoning it excels other doctrines, what its method and order of teaching are, and finally, what its primary parts are. Second, it adds a paraphrase and epitome concerning the sacred names and their attributes. I have rescued these from the library of the deluded Jews (like a most brilliant torch snatched from the hand of a blind man carrying a light) to be handed over to the enlightened minds of the faithful. I have touched upon them in a brief summary, through which the approach to the inner chambers of sacred discourse and the mysteries of the divine names will easily lie open. From this, any perceptive and diligent cultivator of Christian piety will be able, with little trouble, to be initiated into the doctrine of those who use allegory, and in it to profit and be instructed, by the help of divine grace and the nourishing, undivided Trinity. Having invoked its sublime and ineffable name, at which every knee bows, we begin the first part of this Volume. First, however, I have chosen to place here the following speech against a detractor of the Cabala, which brings no small light of understanding to the present task.

<meta>This page continues the "Second Dialogue" between Sophia and Philo. Having previously debated whether the Earth is "ignoble" due to its physical position, Philo now argues that the Earth is actually a nurturing mother to all things. The conversation shifts from the physical elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) to the underlying "Prime Matter" that connects them all through a cycle of birth and change.</meta>

### DIALOGUE II

<margin>All composite things, both animate and inanimate, venerate the earth as their common mother in the manner of children; they are, in turn, loved by her with a maternal affection as if they were her dearest offspring. <note>original: "Omnia mixta tam animata quàm inanimata terram uelut communem matrem filiorū more uenerantur..."</note></margin>
And indeed, the winds, blowing vehemently, strive toward the air; while fiery things, seeking the highest and first of all the elements, climb even higher. Both are driven by a love for their own origin and the element from which they took their beginning, as if from a father. Stones and metals, too, which derive their origin from the earth, are seen to be carried swiftly toward her whenever they are outside of her, never resting until they return. The Earth, moreover, shows the greatest charity by generating, retaining, and conserving them. Furthermore, plants, herbs, and trees pursue the earth, their common mother and creator, with such great love that they never wish to depart from her unharmed; rather, they most zealously embrace her with their roots as if with arms, like infants at their mother’s breasts. The Earth, performing the duty of a pious and diligent mother, does not merely give birth to them—kindled as she is by the greatest charity and enormous love—but she also strives greatly to nourish them and keep them alive by pressing her own internal <term>humor</term> <note>In ancient science, "humors" or fluids were the vital juices—like sap or blood—that sustained life.</note> to the outer surface. In this, she surely imitates a human mother, who sends milk from her vitals to her breasts so that she may provide suitable nourishment for her small children. And if, perhaps by the injury of the seasons or the inclemency of the weather, she becomes too dry and parched, she strives for rain from the sky and air with suppliant vows and most humble prayers. She even risks her own vapors—from which, as they rise, rain-water is made—to purchase and obtain nourishment for her plants and her living creatures. What mother could ever show greater piety and charity toward her children?

**SOPHIA:** It is indeed a marvel that the earth, an inanimate body, should have such great care for her children. We ought to respect much more the one who made the earth so vigilant and hardworking for the safety of her children. It only remains for you to adapt that first reason for the mutual love of animals—which is taken from the desire and pleasure of generating—to the elements and to bodies that lack all sense.

<margin>The love of generating is found quite distinctly in the elements, and moreover in the common matter of all lower things. <note>original: "Amor generandi in elementis, & in cōmunissimā insuper rerū omnium inferio rum materia distinctè admodū reperitur."</note></margin>
**PHILO:** The love of generating is found more extensively and abundantly in the elements and the matter of these lower things than any other love of the higher things.

**SOPHIA:** Why did you just mention "matter" in addition to the simple bodies (the elements)? Is there some other matter of these lower things besides the four elements, from which everything else generated in this lower world is seen to be born?

**PHILO:** This is true indeed; but since we see these same elements being generated everywhere, something must surely be found from which *they* are generated.

**SOPHIA:** From what? Surely one element is generated from another. For we frequently see water made from air, air from water, fire from air, and air from fire. The same must be said of the earth.

<margin>The four elements themselves are the matter and subject of the things that are generated from them. <note>original: "Rerum, quæ ex elementis generantur, ipsamet quatuor elementa sunt materia atq; subiectum."</note></margin>
**PHILO:** This is also true. But of the things generated from the elements, the four elements themselves are the matter and subject; in the thing born from them, these elements remain and are seen, joined and united together by a certain wonderful craftsmanship and power. However, in the mutual generation of the elements, we cannot simply lay one down as the "matter" for the other. For when fire is turned into water, fire does not remain in the water; rather, the fire is "corrupted" <note>In philosophy, "corruption" is the technical term for the ending of one thing's existence so another can begin.</note> and water is generated. Therefore, it is necessary to assign some common "matter" to the elements in which their individual changes can take place—a matter which, for example, having previously put on the form of air when prepared by a suitable alteration, now puts off that form of air and is clothed in the form of water. We must feel exactly the same way about the other exchanges of the elements.

<margin>Prime matter was discovered by natural philosophers because of the mutual exchanges of the four elements.</margin>
<margin>"Chaos" signifies confusion.</margin>
This is called **Prime Matter** by philosophers, and was called **Chaos** by the ancient sages, which signifies "confusion." This is because all things that are generated are contained within it by a certain potential and are folded together confusedly; from this same source, individual things come forth into the light distinctly and in an ordered series.

**SOPHIA:** Truly, what kind of love can be attributed to this matter?

<margin>Prime matter loves all forms as a woman loves a man. <note>original: "Materia prima formas omnes ut fœmina mas"</note></margin>

<summary>Philo explains how the Earth acts as a nurturing mother to all things and introduces the philosophical concept of "Prime Matter" (Chaos), the underlying substance that allows elements like fire and water to transform into one another.</summary>

# THE WORKS OF JOHANNES REUCHLIN
### ON THE CABALISTIC ART, BOOK II.

Time, the circle, the outermost limit of the World, motion, a certain difference or alterity in matter, and that matter is subject to generation and corruption. He taught that **necessity** weighs upon the World; some things happen by necessity, some by fate, some by choice, some by fortune, and some by chance; the cause of these is hidden from human reason, a view in which Anaxagoras also concurs. Our teacher [Pythagoras] also thought the World began from fire. Its right side is in the east, its left in the west. Then, following Thales, he divided the heaven into five zones, then into the equinoxes and solstices (two of each) and the Bear <note>Referring to the Arctic circle, associated with the Great Bear constellation</note>. He divided the globe of the lands likewise. Furthermore, he was the first of all to discover the **obliquity of the zodiac** <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit, which creates the seasons</note> along the Sun's path. He said the Moon appeared to be an ignited terrestrial soil, containing fields, mountains, and valleys. Concerning the soul, he declared it in this way: it is a **self-moving number**, which he distributed through its powers thus: the vital part around the heart, the rational and mental part around the head. The whole soul cannot perish; for the rational part is the work of the eternal God, while the irrational part is corruptible. To the same author [Pythagoras] should be attributed a more true divination regarding sacrifices. He held that human seed is the foam of the most useful blood, belonging to corporeal matter but endowed with incorporeal power. Moreover, the female likewise emits seed. Furthermore, not only man but other living creatures have reason, though without a **mind** <note>Latin: *mens*; Reuchlin distinguishes between basic logic/instinct and the higher intellect</note>. That many of these do not seem to act rationally is surely blamed on a **dyscrasia** <note>original: "dycrasia"; a medical term for an imbalance of bodily fluids or "humors"</note> of their bodies: because they are not endowed with the proper instruments, they do not have words (whether they are tame or wild), but hold certain symbols and certain signs in place of words, by which signs they express their thoughts to one another. Thus, beasts speak but do not "discourse," which the Greeks say more significantly as *to babble indeed, but not to speak with structured meaning* <note>original Greek: λαλεῖν μὲν, οὐ φράζειν δὲ</note>. All those volumes of Plutarch on the opinions of the philosophers are very good witnesses of these things. Concerning the rest of this World, whether substances or accidents, there are almost innumerable writers in every sect of philosophers: some have spoken generally about the nature of the universe, such as Aristotle, Theophrastus, and almost all your Arabs and Moors; others spoke particularly about individual things, such as Julius Pollux, Dioscorides, Pliny, and those like them. Yet almost every later scholar has taken the heads of all disciplines from the treasury of Pythagoras’s philosophy like an heir, and cultivated that inheritance with literary study, and according to the peculiar quality of his own genius, adorned it as much as he was able and extended it with his full strength.

But what does it help to know or hold opinions on all things if they do not take away all sorrow and torment from us in this life, and in the next life—after the absence of evils—add the most abundant gathering of all the good things we have so diligently learned? What does it help, finally, if by knowing well we do evil, and by doing evil we cannot be entirely free from fear and so can enjoy no tranquil state of mind? Or again, if we always carry out orders like beasts of burden, being otherwise in all things foolish, stolid, fatuous, like mushrooms, slow-witted, and dullards, differing nothing from a brute? Therefore, it seemed appropriate to Pythagoras to direct all philosophy toward the peak of longed-for happiness and the ready security of eternal joy, which he placed in the **contemplation of the highest and divine things**. He thought that fruit, as if from a blessed tree, would undoubtedly follow our tireless studies of philosophizing, if we first—our soul having been purged—vehemently turn away from vices and diligently cultivate virtues. Thus, conscious of no evil within ourselves, we might apply ourselves with a joyful mind and cheerful zeal to **mathematical speculations**, which are observed by us as the middle ground between natural and divine things. For they are partly inseparable from matter like natural things, and partly separated like divine things. For a circle or harmony, although it does not exist without matter, is yet understood without matter; indeed, no concern for matter is involved when we handle any mathematical subject. Since, therefore, it was difficult—not to say impossible—for our intellect to leap suddenly from natural to supernatural things and from entirely material to purely immaterial things, Pythagoras therefore wished to provide his disciples with certain...

It concludes by arguing that the ultimate goal of philosophy is happiness through the study of mathematics, which serves as a necessary bridge between the physical and divine realms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument of Capnion (Reuchlin’s persona) regarding the power of divine names. He is moving from a general discussion of "virtue" to the specific transition between the Old Testament's silent, ineffable name of God (the Tetragrammaton) and the New Testament's spoken name of the incarnate Word.</meta>

...[it seems] hard, if not impossible. But it is difficult for us to be moved by a voice from the ineffable <note>In this context, "the ineffable" refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God (YHWH) which was considered too sacred to be spoken aloud.</note>, which we might use obediently, or which might be ready and at hand for us in any circumstance, any emotion, or any danger. Therefore, what remains is that, led by necessity, we turn with keen judgment to examine the named voices, if first we investigate as briefly as possible, with a somewhat deeper study, the cause of such great power and such virtue in names. For this reason, it seemed best to act more openly now. For just as the mercy of the sky, the rays of the stars, and the eternal fires of the heavenly bodies are believed to effect something in things below the moon by their downward flow:

> From this we can foretell the storms in the doubtful sky,
> From this the day of harvest and the time of sowing,
> And when it is fitting to lash the treacherous sea with oars,
> When to launch the armed fleets,
> Or to fell the pine tree in the woods at its season.
> Not in vain do we watch the settings and risings of the constellations,
> And the year made equal across four different seasons.

This is the work of nature, this the influence of rays, this descent of light, motion, and heat penetrating all things with subtle vivacity. Hence, as the same Mantuan poet <note>Virgil, who was born near Mantua.</note> says:

> The appearances of their minds are turned, and their breasts
> Conceive new movements—some now, others while the wind
> Drove the clouds; hence that chorus of birds in the fields,
> And the joyful cattle, and the ravens exulting with their throats.

And, to be brief, just as the nature of the universe acts naturally upon individual things according to its prescribed order, so the preeminent mistress of nature, the cause of all things—the divine will—acts supernaturally upon each and every thing through its limitless grace. And just as those natural things act through the medium of sensible qualities, so this divine will acts sometimes through the medium of intellectual names in a confederated way, without proportion, without similarity, and without measuring the cause against the effects. This is what God taught us through heavenly revelation via Isaiah. "For as the rain and snow come down from heaven," he says, "and do not return thither, but soak the earth and water it, making it sprout and giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things for which I sent it." 

<margin>THE WORD OF GOD.</margin> Since therefore from the higher things, as I believe, the Word of God (which is called by another name "reason," since both are expressed by the Greeks with one word, <term>Logos <note>original: λόγος</note></term>) clearly appeared to us to be that by which God makes all things, and works all things in heaven, on earth, and in all the depths. Regarding this, I pray you, listen even to the mathematician Marcus Manilius in his *Astronomica* <note>A 1st-century AD Latin poem on astrology and astronomy.</note> addressed to Augustus, who says in his poem:

> This work, constructed of the body of the immense world,
> And the members of nature established in diverse forms—
> The force of the divine soul rules the air, the fire, the earth, and the lying sea;
> God conspires with a sacred path and governs with silent reason,
> And dispenses many covenants to every part.

also <term>caput</term> with <term>occiduum</term>, and hence this <term>occaput, -itis</term>, i.e., the western and last part, the head. It is said <term>occaput</term> is composed of <term>ob</term> and <term>caput</term>, and hence it is called <term>occaput</term> as if it were <term>capite retroflu</term> <gloss>flowing back from the head</gloss>. And the same as <term>occipitis</term>. Also it is composed with <term>sincerus</term> and it is called <term>sinaput, -itis</term>, i.e., the anterior part of the head. With absence. Also [it is] pure and open because of the absence of hair. Also it is composed with <term>par</term>, [and] it is called <term>parceps</term> and with <term>anceps</term> [meaning] two-headed.

<term>Carabrio, -onis</term> is a kind of bird similar to a weasel.

<term>Carabus</term> <gloss>Small boat</gloss>, a small boat made from wicker and covered with raw leather, so that it may be a boat to run with on a river. Also it is named [for] that which is in the middle of a ship.

<term>Character, -ris</term>, Greek: image, new look, likeness, form. Or a stylus, figure, letter, the iron with which a mark is burnt onto cattle. It is named <term>character</term> [for] the mark itself or sign.

<term>Characterismus, -i</term>, is a description of someone's form.

<term>Caradrion</term> is a certain bird, entirely white, whose entrails heal dim eyes. If the sick person is to live, it will approach him; if he is to die, it flees from him. It is said to fly through the middle of the nights high in the sky.

<term>Charagma, -tis</term>, i.e., impression, image, or letter. It is said [as in] Lucian: "Thus the number has the <term>charagma</term> <gloss>mark</gloss> of Caesar; thus man has the <term>charagma</term> of God."

<term>Charaxis, -is</term>, i.e., notation, and named from <term>character</term>.

<term>Carbafus, -i</term>, in the singular; in the plural <term>carbasa</term>, feminine gender, i.e., a veil, [so named because it] lacks a <term>basis</term>, i.e., a support from the lower part. <term>Carbafus</term> is also called a certain kind of linen garment, which can fit both a man and a woman. But <term>carbafas, -atis</term> pertains to the sails of ships, and the middle syllable is common. Ovid says: "I gave the <term>carbasa</term> <gloss>sails</gloss> stretched by the south wind."

<term>Carto, -onis</term> <gloss>Charcoal</gloss>, named from <term>carpo</term>, because it is plucked from fire, or rather named from <term>careo, -es</term>, because it lacks flame. And when it is kindled it is called an ember; when the ember is extinguished it is called <term>carto</term>. <term>Cartonarius, -ii</term> [is one] who makes charcoal. It is said: Charcoal <gloss>carto</gloss> lacks flame, once the ember is extinguished it is called [charcoal].

<term>Carbūculus, -i</gloss> <gloss>Carbuncle/Garnet</gloss>, both for a small coal and for a precious stone ignited like a coal, whose brilliance does not stop even in the night. And for a certain disease it is found, because it is red in its origin like fire, afterwards black like extinguished coal. It is said: And the stone is for the disease, the carbuncle coal stands forth.

<term>Carcanus</term>, the name of a city or place.

<term>Carcan, Calcamo, Arphat, Emath</term>, are cities in the East.

<term>Carcer</term>, in the singular, properly named where the guilty are bound. But in the plural, whence chariots are released, or the barriers placed in front, and <term>carcer</term> is named as capturing the guilty,

<column-break/>

and it is etymology, not composition. In <term>carcerarius, -ii</term> [one] who makes or guards a prison. In this and that <term>carceralis</term> [adjective].

<term>Carchesia</term>, cups from the place Carchesium, or a cave, or the summit of the mast of a ship. It is said in Greek. But you would say <term>carchesia</term> is an instrument of a ship. It is said [to be] a wheel through which ropes are drawn. Also certain vessels made to the likeness of those [things] are called <term>carchesia</term>. Also wheels are called [so], [as] they have wheels. For <term>crochos</term> is said in Greek, <term>rota</term> <gloss>wheel</gloss> in Latin. Also <term>carchesia</term> [is] the summit of the mast, in which cords meet. Lucan says: "And I wish it would bend the <term>carchesia</term> of the top of the mast."

<term>Cardiacus, -a, -um</term>, [middle syllable] short, i.e., suffering from a beating of the heart as if the heart is burning because of slime. And named from <term>ardeo</term> and <term>cor</term> by composition. Or from the Greek <term>cardia</term>, which is heart. Juvenal says: "Never to send a cup to a <term>cardiacus</term> <gloss>heart-sufferer</gloss> friend." Or it is composed from <term>cor</term> and <term>bios</term>, as if heart-having because of slime, and then it is named <term>cordiacus</term>.

<term>Cardia</term> in Greek, in Latin [is] heart.

<term>Cardinalis</term>, [adjective], and this [adjective], and <term>cardinarius, -a, -um</term> in the same sense, namely that which pertains to a hinge. It is said the cardinal winds are named [as] blowing from the four parts of the world. And certain virtues are called cardinal to the likeness of a hinge, on which the motion of a door is fastened. And this <term>cardinalis</term> [is used] substantively for a name of dignity, because by the cardinals the world ought to be ruled and governed [and] moved, just as a door [is moved] by a hinge.

<term>Cardo, -inis</term>, of uncertain gender, named for one part of the door, namely the pivot which turns in the hole, or it is placed for the hole itself sometimes. And named from <term>cardia</term>, which is heart, because as the heart rules and moves men, so that pivot rules and moves the door. <term>Cardo</term> is also named the extremity of a thing. It is said the hinges of the sky are named the extreme parts of the axis, thus named, because by them the heavens turn. <term>Cardo</term> is also placed for opportunity or critical moment. Virgil says: "Or the matter is at such a <term>cardo</term>," i.e., in a critical moment or opportunity. Virgil says: "Or the king will delay at such a hinge." But <term>cardo, -onis</term> is an herb harmful to farmers, i.e., thistle. It is said: The thistle <term>cardo</term> is present at the doors if the thistle is pleasing. But <term>cardo, -onis</term> is an herb harmful to farmers.

<term>Cardomomum, -i</gloss>, is a certain herb, a certain grain, a species of spice.

<term>Carduelis, -is</gloss> <gloss>Goldfinch</gloss>, is a certain bird named from <term>carduus</term> <gloss>thistle</gloss>, because it feeds on thistles and cardoons.

<term>Cardularii indices</term> <gloss>Cardularian judges</gloss> were called formerly those who had power from the emperor of judging, and those who chose to litigate before them; and they could choose without the consent of the prior judge, thus it is handed down.

<term>Nicola</term>: a name of people. And it is interpreted as "victory of the people," that is, victors who are popular and vile. And <term>nice</term> <gloss>Greek: Nike</gloss> is victory, and <term>laos</term> <gloss>Greek: Laos</gloss> is people. <term>Dñ</term> <gloss>Dominus/Master</gloss> <term>Grealis</term>: since <term>laos</term> is the people, it shows [it] regarding <term>Ninyctages</term>, heretics, so called from <term>nū</term> and <term>colaus</term> <note>likely referring to Nicotians/Nicolaitans</note>, because they reject the night vigils, being superstitious, violating divine laws which grant the night for rest.
<term>Nyctalīn</term>: a certain passion which denies sight during the day with open eyes, and restores it when the night shadows rush in. And conversely, it restores sight, and denies [it] at night. And it comes from <term>nyctos</term> <gloss>Greek: night</gloss>, which is night. See <term>nyctalinic</term>: one who suffers from such a disease.
<term>Nyctamen</term>: a vigil.
<term>Nycticorax</term>: by some, an owl, which is also called a <term>bubo</term> <gloss>horned owl</gloss>. But some say it is the night-owl, which flies at night, from <term>nyctos</term>, which is night, and <term>corax</term>, which is crow, because it is like a night-crow, because it flies at night, as it keeps watch at night.
<term>Nyctilus</term>: nocturnal. And it comes from <term>nyctos</term>, which is night. Also <term>nyctilins</term> <gloss>Bacchic</gloss>, from Bacchus, because they sacrificed at night, or they were given to drinking and getting drunk at night.
<term>Nyctimene</term>: an owl.
<term>Nychuius</term>: <term>nyctos</term> in Greek is said as night in Latin.
<term>Nyctaus</term>: a vigil, or a movement of the eyelids.
<term>Nidor</term>: an odor, especially of roasting.
<term>Nidulus</term>: a small nest. Whence Job 30: "In my nest I shall die."
<term>Nidus</term>: a habitation of birds, woven together from various twigs.
<term>Nigellus</term>: somewhat black. Also <term>nigellus</term> is another diminutive.
<term>Niger</term>: from <term>nubiger</term>, that is, bearing clouds and obscurity. And also from <term>nubes</term>, because it is not serene, but covered with darkness. And it is seen to be a compound. Also <term>niger</term> is compounded into <term>subniger</term>, that is, somewhat black.
<term>Nihili</term>: nothing. And by apocope, <term>nihil</term>, indeclinable, from which by syncope comes <term>nil</term>, indeclinable. And see <term>nihilū</term>, as if <term>no bitum</term>, that is, no piece <note>referring to the etymology of 'ni-hilum'</note>. And one finds <term>nihilis</term> or <term>hilis</term>; see that trifle which is on a quill, which is of no value. Also one finds <term>nihili</term> indeclinable, or rather it is a genitive of value <note>referring to the genitive of price</note>, and figuratively it is construed with any case or gender, as it is construed in a transitive way, such as <term>nihili homo</term>, <term>nihili hominis</term>, <term>nihili homini</term>, etc., that is, of no utility, or price, or value of a man. And the aforesaid should be written with 'h' and 'l'.
<term>Niliae</term>: pertaining to the Nile, as Egyptian. And it comes from <term>Nilus</term>. And <term>niloticus</term> in the same sense. Whence Lucan in [book] 9: "The king holding the impure Nilotic realms."

<column-break/>

<term>Niligena</term>: born from the Nile, or in Egypt.
<term>Nilotis</term>: Egyptian. And it comes from <term>Nilus</term>.
<term>Nilns</term> <note>Nilus</note>: the river of Egypt. It is said thus, as if <term>nilum</term>, that is, drawing mud which effects fertility.
<term>Nimbus</term>: the density of a cloud in a dark storm. And it comes from <term>nubes</term>. And they are <term>nimbi</term> <note>perhaps meant 'nimble'</note>, slow and huge, as if flowing. Also <term>nimbosus</term>: tempestuous, cloudy. And hence <term>nimbus</term>: wind mixed with water. Also a <term>nimbus</term> is a transverse band of gold sewn into linen, which is on the forehead of women. Also <term>nimbosus</term> <note>in the sense of being adorned</note>: adorned with a nimbus.
<term>Nimmurus</term>: a husband whose wife commits adultery and he remains silent.
<term>Nympha</term>: generally of waters, and especially of fountains. And it comes from <term>nubes</term>, because waters come from the clouds and have their origin [there]. And <term>nymphe</term> are said to be the same as the Muses, and not without merit; for the movement of water creates a muse <note>sound</note>. Also <term>nympha</term> is the water itself. Also <term>nympha</term> is a bride in nuptials, said for the office of washing, which also alludes to the name <term>nubes</term>. Whence Ovid: "They bear grateful vows to the nymphs." And it is compounded with <term>para</term>, which is 'beside', and see <term>paranympha</term> <gloss>bridesmaid</gloss>.
<term>Ringidus</term> <note>Rigidus</note>: stiff, cold.
<term>Nifus</term> <note>Nixus</term>: an effort. And it comes from <term>nitor</term>. And <term>nifus</term> is a participle. Also this <term>nilus</term> is a bird, which by another name is called <term>alietus</term> <gloss>osprey</gloss>, and it is said to be from King Nifus of Megara, who was changed into that bird, as in the fables of the poets.
<term>Nisi</term> is a conjunction. Whence one: "There are no wounds except from a divine dart." "The daughter of the snows is not safe except without Nifus <note>a play on words</note>."
<term>Nitedula</term>: a certain animal, as if fire shining in the night, and it comes from <term>niteo</term>.
<term>Nitella</term>: a small <term>nito</term> <gloss>marten or weasel</gloss>.
<term>Nitens</term>: participle from <term>niteo</term>, shining, sparkling, splendid. Also <term>nitens</term>, participle from <term>nitor</term>, that is, leaning, laboring. Whence <term>enites</term>, <term>renites</term>.
<term>Nitidus</term>: splendid, clear, adorned, cultured, proper. And it comes from <term>niteo</term>. Hence <term>nitiditas</term>: splendor.
<term>Nitoi</term> <note>Nitor</note>: splendor, whiteness. It comes from <term>niteo</term>.
<term>Nitru</term>: a certain species of earth with minute threads.

the constitution of a prince <note>original: "principis vtilata cora .p.cribo sacri palatij"</note> of the sacred palace: a constitution which an emperor establishes or ordains by the counsel of his court. It is also every confirmation made in writing by the emperor with the investigation of a case regarding a contract of exchange, as in the Digest, Book "On the King's Exchange," in the gloss. And a pragmatic sanction of the sacred palace is a rescript of the prince, as in the chapter "Foundations" regarding elections, Book 6.

Pragmaticaries are those who write pragmatic sanctions. In another way, they are called secretaries, or masters of the registry, or registry memorialists, because the writing of the sanction obtained is kept polished in the registry for memory.

Prandeum: a certain noun; and it is a <term>prandium</term> <gloss>midday meal</gloss>.

Prandium, -dii: as if <term>paratum</term> <gloss>prepared</gloss>, from the apparatus of eating, because more is prepared in the morning than in the evening for eating. And formerly, the meals of all soldiers were called <term>prandia</term>, namely food before a fight, as if quickly prepared. But now, it is every meal in the third hour. Hence this <term>prandiolum, -li</term>, a diminutive: a small meal.

Prasium, -ii, neuter gender: a common or place where leeks <note>original: "pĩa" — likely short for "porra" (leeks)</note> are eaten <note>original: "pransus.sa.fu"</note>. It is taken actively, that is, one who eats leeks, and then it descends from <term>prandeo, -ere</term>. Also, it is taken passively: <term>pransus</term>, that is, eaten, which is eaten; and then it descends from the passive of this verb, which is found in the third person, namely <term>prandetur</term>, <term>prandebatur</term>.

Prasis or <term>prasim</term> in Greek is "green" in Latin.

Prasius, -sia, -sium: green; and <term>prasis</term> is all. And this <term>prasius</term> is called a green stone.

Pratum, -ti, neuter gender: a place where grasses grow for the nourishment of domestic animals. Or a field without heavy labor and much cultivation, providing grasses, and it is called <term>pratum</term> as if <term>paratum</term> <gloss>prepared</gloss>, because it requires little labor of cultivation. Also <term>pratellum, -li</term>, <term>pratulum, -li</term>. And this and this <term>pratelis</term> and this <term>pratum</term> <term>paratum</term>; some are castrated <note>note: likely referring to the nature of the ground or a specific botanical classification</note> because it abounds in meadow grass, or because it was constructed in a meadow.

Also this and this <term>pratelis</term> is a gentile noun.

Pravicors, -cordis, of all genders: one with a depraved heart or of a depraved heart. Lord, Ecclesiasticus 3: "A perverse heart <note>original: "Prauicors"</note> will be scandalized in them." This is a correction of books and correctors. Rabanus: "The perverse-hearted."

Pravus, -a, -um: bad and twisted. But a bad person is naturally <term>pravus</term> by exercise and use, and prolong this syllable, "bra." Lord, some say: "I desire the pleasing man; the perverse man is hateful, well." Who becomes nothing, no one pleases the perverse man.

Preambulus, -la, -lum: one walking before <note>note: Latin "ambulans"</note>, which can also be placed substantively.

Prebenda, -ae: <note>note: etymological gloss regarding "papiedi"</note>, it pertains to a collegiate church from the action of providing what is competent to someone as one of the college, who receives it by right and canonically. For there should not be a canonry without a prebend, as in the chapter "Relati," in the same title. And it proceeds from this...

<column-break/>

...tution and office, for from the things that he does, the office owes a prebend and a benefice to the priest. Also, <term>prebenda</term> is taken broadly for the right which is granted to someone, not as to a member of a college, but by reason of a ministry or office, or granted for utility, by using and enjoying certain things of the church for his lifetime, such as the revenues which canons receive, or others. And laymen, especially nobles, have such prebends.

Prebendarius, -ria, -rium: that which pertains to a prebend.

Prebendarius, -rii: one who gives a prebend, or one who can receive one.

Prebendula, -le, diminutive: a small prebend.

Precarius, -ria, -rium: <term>precabilis</term> <gloss>that which can be prayed for</gloss>. Or <term>precarium</term> is whatever is obtained by prayer, which is <term>precadium</term>, which is heard by prayer; and the etymology seems to be rather than composition. Hence <term>precarie</term>, an adverb, that is, <term>precabiliter</term> <gloss>prayerfully</gloss>, or by prayers. And for it, <term>precario</term> is often found. Lord, Terence in the Eunuch: "Even if you ask for it as a favor <note>original: "precario"</note>," according to Huguccio.

Papias says: <term>Precarium</term> is that which, having been requested by the creditor's prayer, permits the debtor to linger in the possession of the land obligated to him and to take the fruits, called as if <term>precadium</term>, because it is heard by prayer.

<term>Precarium</term> according to Accursius in his notes is that which is granted by the owners to the one asking, for so long as the one who granted it allows. But according to Goffredus, it is that pledge obligated to a creditor and granted by the creditor to the debtor himself to be used, which the one who granted it allows. As is from the law "The First," on <term>precarium</term>, Digest, where Ulpian says that this kind of liberty descends from the law of nations. And he adds in the same place: <term>Precarium</term> differs from a donation, because one who donates gives so that he does not receive that which he gives; but one who grants a <term>precarium</term> does not yield it so that he does not receive it back whenever it pleases him.

Or <term>precarium</term> is a contract between the owner and the tenant, and it is a gratuitous contract and similar to a loan, to the extent that some would say these contracts do not differ except in words, although they also differ in the thing. For although it is agreed in many ways in <term>precarium</term> and loan, <term>precarium</term> still differs from a loan, for a loan is made for a certain use, and it cannot be revoked until the use is fulfilled. But <term>precarium</term> can be revoked whenever it pleases. Also, <term>precarium</term> is a contract to be revoked from five-year period to five-year period. And if, after the five-year period has elapsed, it is continued by silence, such a contract is understood to be revoked. It is called <term>precarium</term> for that reason, because it is a contract made at prayers.

<term>Precaria</term> is a donation made at prayers until the death of the recipient. See 11, question 1; 16, question 3, "Regarding the Cleric." And that contract is akin to emphyteusis <gloss>long-term lease</gloss>. Also <term>precarie</term> are called certain payments or concessions of usufruct made at prayers in compensation for that property which is conferred to the church, the form of which is held in 10, question 2, "Precarie."

Precator, -toris: a requester. Hence <term>precatrix</term>, -tricis.

Hence <term>madidus, -a, -um</term>, that is, humid. And <term>madefco, -fais</term> <gloss>inchoative</gloss>, that is, I begin to be moist. And <term>madeo</term> lacks a supine, and shorten the <term>ma</term>. <note>In Lucan, in the first [book]:</note> Lucan, in the first:
"The walls have become moist with fraternal blood."
And <term>madeo</term> is compounded with <term>facio</term>, as <note><term>Madefacio, -cis</term>, that is, to make humid.</note> <term>Madefacio, -cis</term>, that is, to make humid. And with <term>fio</term>, as <note><term>Madefio</term></note> <term>Madefio</term>, that is, to become humid. Also with <term>con</term>, as <term>comadeo</term>. Also with <term>de</term>, as <term>demadeo</term>, that is, to be greatly moist downward. Also with <term>vi</term>, <term>con</term>, and <term>in</term> for <term>e</term>.
<term>Madido, -vas, -daui</term>, to make moist.
<term>Magistro, -tras, -as</term>, to teach, and shorten the first. <note>Lord Cato:</note> Lord Cato: "You will find something that teaches you to avoid."
<term>Magnifico, -as, -aui</term>, to make great, to exalt, to commend, and it is said from <term>magnus</term> <gloss>great</gloss> and <term>facio</term>.
<term>Maioro, -as, -aui</term>, to make greater, and lengthen the <term>io</term>.
<term>Malefacio, -cis, -feci, -cti</term>, <term>neuter</term> <term>transitive</term>, to do evil.
<term>Maligno, -as, -aui</term>, <term>neuter</term> <term>passive</term>, to do malignly, or rather to make malignant, and to molest. And in the same sense comes <term>malignoz, -ari</term> <gloss>deponent</gloss>.
<term>Malleo, -as, -aui</term>, to beat with a hammer. Hence <term>malleator</term>: look at the blacksmith.
<term>Malo, -mauis, -mauult, -malui, -malle</term>, <term>neuter</term> <term>gender</term>, that is, to wish more. And it is compounded from the adverb <term>magis</term> <gloss>more</gloss> and <term>volo, -vis</term>.
<term>Manacipo, -pas, -pauia</term>, to serve, as to reduce into servitude, or to make a slave <gloss>mancipium</gloss>. And <term>mancipare</term>, that is, to draw by hand, or to give, or to lead. And it is placed simply for to give, or to lead. And it is thus active; but for to serve, it is neuter, and shorten the <term>pe</term>.
<term>Mando, -vas, -daui</term>, to command. And <term>mandare</term>, that is, to send. <note>Lord:</note> Lord: "He who sends, commands; he who orders, commands." And you note that <term>mando</term> sometimes in composition changes <term>a</term> into <term>e</term>, as <note><term>Amendo</term></note> <term>Amendo, -vas</term> and <term>comendo, -vas</term>. Sometimes it retains <term>a</term>, as <term>remando, -vas</term>. <note>Lord James 2:8:</note> Lord James 2:8: "Command, send back."
<term>Mado, -vis, -vi, -sum</term>, <term>neuter</term> <term>transitive</term>, to eat. <note>Lord Job 30:</note> Lord Job 30: <note>He was eating herbs and the barks of trees.</note> "He was eating herbs and the barks of trees." Hence this masculine and feminine <term>mandibilis</term>, and this neuter <term>le</term>.
<term>Manduco, -cas, -cauia</term>, to eat, and it is said from <term>manduc</term>, and lengthen the <term>pe</term>. <note>Lord:</note> Lord: "You can eat the ant if you take off the head."
<term>Manco, -nes, -si</term>, <term>neuter</term> <term>substantive</term>, to delay. And <term>mane</term>, to await, and thus it is construed with the accusative. <note>Lord Acts 20:</note> Lord Acts 20: <note>Dangers and tribulations await me.</note> "Dangers and tribulations await me." <note>Lord: He who remains awaits, and he who awaits, that one delays.</note>
<term>Manico, -cas, -cau</term>, <term>neuter</term> <term>passive</term>, to hasten, to go in the morning, to arise early, or to convene, and it is said from <term>mane</term> <gloss>morning</gloss>. <note>A certain gloss says on that Luke 21:</note> A certain gloss says on that Luke 21: <note>The people were coming together to him in the morning; that is, he was accelerating to come.</note> "The people were coming together to him in the morning; that is, he was accelerating to come." And lengthen the first <term>ma</term>.
<term>Manifesto, -tas</term>, to publish. Hence <term>manifestarius, -a, -um</term>, who manifests, or who is manifested, or doing something manifest.

<column-break/>

<term>Mano, -nas, -naui</term>, <term>neuter</term> <term>passive</term>, to flow, to run down. And it is compounded <term>comano, -as</term>, <note><term>Demano, -as</term>.</note> <term>Demano, -as</term>. <term>Emano, -as</term>. <term>Permano, -as</term>. And lengthen <term>ma</term>. <note>Lord</note> Lord Gratius in the Poetria: <note>From the full vessel it flows from the body.</note> "From the full vessel it flows from the body." But <term>maneo, -nes</term> shortens <term>ma</term>. <note>Lord:</note> Lord: "If the vice remains, the drop of tears remains for you. Do well what remains, because the plague remains for you."
<term>Manfito, -tas</term>, to remain frequently, and is said from <term>manfo, -fas</term>, and shorten the <term>fi</term> according to <note>Rug.</note> Rug. Papias, however, says: <note><term>Manfitat</term>, that is, he frequently remains.</note> "<term>Manfitat</term>, that is, he frequently remains."
